title: The Sea and the Coast
description: Ten stories and short texts from the American coast: a lighthouse keeper, a fish merchant, a sailing course, sea turtles, whales, a sand castle contest, a harbor museum and a town debating the future of its harbor.

lessons.title: The Keeper of Stone Point
lessons.summary: After 31 years, a lighthouse keeper in Maine retires, and the whole town gathers to thank him.
lessons.text:
For 31 years, Walter Hayes lived in the small white house beside the lighthouse at Stone Point, on the coast of Maine. Every evening he climbed the narrow stairs to the top of the tower and made sure that the great light was working. Every morning he wrote a few lines in a thick notebook: the wind, the weather and the ships he had seen during the night.

Walter loved to observe the sea, and he could observe it for hours without getting bored. In summer the water was calm and blue, and the reflection of the clouds lay on it like a painting. In winter it turned dark and wild, and heavy waves broke against the rocks below the house. On peaceful nights he sat by the window with a cup of tea and watched the long beam of light move slowly across the water. To Walter, there was no more peaceful place in the world.

This year, however, Walter turned 70, and he decided that it was time to retire. The light no longer needed a keeper, because a computer could now turn it on and off. "I could have stayed a few more years," he told his daughter, Ruth, "but I would rather retire while I still enjoy the work."

On his last evening, the whole town gathered at Stone Point. Fishermen, teachers, children and old friends gathered on the grass in front of the house. Ruth had written a short speech, and although she was nervous, she stayed calm and composed as she read it. She said that her father had made a promise when he was young: to keep the light burning for every boat at sea. "He fulfilled that promise every single night," she said, "in fog, in snow and in storms."

Then Walter spoke. He was usually a quiet man, and his voice shook a little at first, but soon he was composed again. He thanked the town and said that wherever he lived from now on, he would always hear the sound of the waves. "Wherever I go," he said, "part of me will stay here."

Walter is not moving far. He has bought a small house in town with a garage, and in the garage he keeps his old wooden boat. He plans to repair it this winter, so that he can fulfill one last wish. In spring he wants to sail out past Stone Point and look at the reflection of the light on the water, the way sailors always did.

Questions:
How long did Walter live beside the lighthouse?
He lived there for 31 years.
What did Walter love to observe?
He loved to observe the sea, and he could observe it for hours.
Why did Walter decide to retire this year?
He turned 70, and the light no longer needed a keeper, because a computer could turn it on and off.
Who gathered at Stone Point on his last evening?
Fishermen, teachers, children and old friends gathered on the grass in front of the house.
What promise had Walter fulfilled?
He had kept the light burning for every boat at sea, every single night.
What does Walter keep in his garage?
He keeps his old wooden boat in his garage.

lessons.title: The Fish Merchant of Harbor Street
lessons.summary: A fish merchant in a Massachusetts fishing town chooses her fish with care and sells her mother's fish pie.
lessons.text:
Every morning at 5, before the sun is up, Rosa Costa walks down to the harbor in Port Hollis, a fishing town in Massachusetts. Her family has been in the fish business for three generations. Her grandfather was a fisherman, but her father became a merchant, and now Rosa is a fish merchant too. She buys fish straight from the boats and sells it in her small shop on Harbor Street.

The boats come in with the first gray light, their decks wet and shining. Rosa never pays for fish unless she has looked at it carefully. She checks the eyes, which should be clear, and the smell, which should be fresh and clean, like the sea itself. If the quality is excellent, she buys a large quantity. If it is only acceptable, she buys a smaller quantity, because she would rather sell out early than offer her customers fish that is merely acceptable.

The rules for selling fish are strict, and Rosa thinks they should be strict. An inspector visits her shop twice a year, and every spring she has to renew her license at the town office. Last month she went there to renew it once again. "Strict rules protect everyone," she says. "They protect the customers, and they protect the fish in the sea, too." There are also limits on the quantity of cod that each boat may catch, so that the fish do not disappear.

In the shop, Rosa works quickly with a long, sharp knife. She can slice a large fish into perfect pieces in less than a minute. Customers often ask her to slice the fish thin for frying or thick for the grill.

On Fridays, Rosa also sells her mother's famous fish pie. The main ingredient, of course, is fresh fish, but the pie also contains potatoes, butter, onions and a little cream. Rosa will not tell anyone her mother's secret ingredient. "If I told you, it would not be a secret," she says with a smile. The pies are usually gone by noon.

When a customer is satisfied, he or she comes back, and Rosa believes that this is the best sign of a good merchant. One old man has bought a slice of fish pie from her shop every Friday for 20 years. "I am a hard man to please," he likes to say, "but here I am always satisfied."

Questions:
What does Rosa do for a living?
She is a fish merchant, like her father.
When does Rosa buy a large quantity of fish?
She buys a large quantity when the quality is excellent.
What does Rosa have to do every spring?
She has to renew her license at the town office.
Why does Rosa think the rules should be strict?
She thinks strict rules protect the customers and the fish in the sea.
What are the ingredients of the fish pie?
It contains fresh fish, potatoes, butter, onions, a little cream and a secret ingredient.
How does Rosa know that her customers are satisfied?
She knows they are satisfied because they come back.

lessons.title: A Kindergarten Goes to the Beach
lessons.summary: A kindergarten teacher takes her class to the beach, where the children explore the shore and draw what they find.
lessons.text:
Ellen Moreno teaches kindergarten in a small town on the coast of Connecticut. On a bright morning in June, she took her kindergarten class of 18 children to the beach for the day. It was their first trip of the year outside the classroom, and the children had talked about nothing else for a week.

Planning a trip with 18 small children is not simple. First, the school administrator had to agree to the plan. The administrator, Mr. Lewis, asked many questions. How many adults would come? Where would the children eat? What would happen if it rained? In the end he agreed, and four parents offered to help. Ellen also packed extra clothes in case someone got wet.

When they arrived at the beach, there was a moment of chaos. Some children ran toward the water, two lost their shoes in the sand, and one boy began to cry because there was sand in his sandwich. Ellen blew a small whistle and asked everyone to gather around her. "When I blow the whistle," she said, "everybody comes and we gather here, next to the big rock." Slowly the chaos ended, and the day could begin.

The children worked in small groups, like little teams of scouts. Each group received a paper pad and a pencil. Their job was to scout the beach for interesting things and draw them on their pads. They found shells, smooth stones, a crab shell and a long white feather. One girl, Lily, drew a tiny crab so carefully that her pad looked like a page from a science book.

Later, Ellen showed them a large rock with thin white lines in it. She explained that the lines were minerals, and that sea water also has minerals in it, such as salt. The children tasted a drop of sea water from their fingers and made funny faces. "It tastes like tears!" one boy shouted.

Near the end of the day, a few boys began climbing on the rocks like monkeys. Ellen asked them to come down. "You are not monkeys," she said kindly, "and wet rocks are dangerous." The boys climbed down at once.

The next morning, back in the classroom, the children put their drawings on the classroom wall in one long line, under a sign that said "Our Day at the Sea." Mr. Lewis, the administrator, came to look at them, and he said it was the most beautiful wall in the whole school.

Questions:
What does Ellen teach?
She teaches kindergarten in a small town in Connecticut.
Who had to say yes to the trip?
The school administrator, Mr. Lewis, had to agree to it.
Why was there chaos when they arrived at the beach?
There was chaos because children ran toward the water, two lost their shoes and one boy found sand in his sandwich.
What did Ellen do to make the children gather around her?
She blew a small whistle.
What did each group receive?
Each group received a paper pad and a pencil to draw what they found.
What did Ellen explain about the white lines in the rock?
She explained that the lines were minerals, and that sea water has minerals too, such as salt.
Where did the children put their drawings?
They put them on the classroom wall.

lessons.title: Learning to Sail
lessons.summary: An office worker from Boston takes a week-long sailing course in Rhode Island and learns to work with the wind.
lessons.text:
My name is David, and last summer I finally did something I had wanted to do for years: I signed up for a sailing course for amateurs. I am 35, I work in an office in Boston, and before the course I knew nothing about boats. I was a complete amateur, and so were the other five people in my group.

The course took place in Newport, Rhode Island, on a wide, quiet bay. On the first morning our instructor, a tall woman named Joan, looked at our clothes and shook her head. "You need to be properly equipped," she said. "The sea does not care how you feel." She gave each of us a life jacket and a heavy coat with a hood. The sun was shining, so I asked, "Um, do we really need the hood?" Joan smiled. "Ask me again in an hour."

An hour later, the wind was much stronger, and cold water was flying over the side of the boat. I pulled the hood over my head and was glad to be well equipped. Our small boat began to bounce over the waves, and every time it hit one, we were thrown against each other. At first I was afraid, but soon I began to enjoy the way the boat would bounce and then rise again.

In my group there was a young man named Pieter, who came from the Netherlands. He told us that in the Netherlands many children learn to sail almost as soon as they can walk. "Um, not me," he said, laughing. "My family preferred bicycles."

Joan was a patient teacher. "You cannot make the wind behave," she said, "but you can learn how it behaves and work with it." She also warned us about the sun. On the water, she explained, the sun's radiation is much stronger, because the water sends the light back up at you. Radiation can burn your skin even when the sky is gray, so we all wore hats and long sleeves.

At the end of the week, each of us had a short evaluation. Joan watched as we sailed alone across the bay and back. I was nervous, but my evaluation went well, and Joan wrote that I was ready for the next level.

People sometimes ask me about my motivation. Why would an office worker spend his vacation getting wet and cold? My motivation is simple. For a few hours on the water, I forget about emails and meetings and think only about the wind.

Questions:
Why did David need the hood after all?
He needed it because the wind grew stronger and cold water flew over the side of the boat.
Where did Pieter come from?
He came from the Netherlands.
What did Joan say about the wind?
She said that you cannot make the wind behave, but you can learn how it behaves and work with it.
Why is the sun's radiation stronger on the water?
It is stronger because the water sends the light back up at you.
How did David's evaluation go?
It went well, and Joan wrote that he was ready for the next level.
What is David's motivation for sailing?
On the water he forgets about emails and meetings and thinks only about the wind.

lessons.title: Morning Patrol for Sea Turtles
lessons.summary: A marine biologist and her volunteers protect sea turtle nests in North Carolina and care for a sick young turtle.
lessons.text:
Dr. Maya Brooks is a marine scientist who studies sea turtles on the coast of North Carolina. From May to August, female turtles come out of the ocean at night to lay their eggs in the sand. Each one digs a deep hole, lays about 100 eggs, covers them and slowly returns to the water. Maya's job is to protect these nests.

Every morning at first light, volunteers patrol the beach. They walk slowly along the shore and look for the wide tracks that a turtle leaves in the sand. When a volunteer finds a nest, she marks it with four small wooden posts and records its position on a tablet. The tablet sends the information straight to Maya's office, so that she always knows where every nest is. Without these patrols, many nests would be destroyed by cars, dogs or people who do not notice them.

Maya gives the volunteers one strict rule: they must never interact with the animals. "Watch them and take photos from a distance, but never touch them," she tells every new group. "When people try to interact with a wild animal, they usually do more harm than good."

This summer Maya is also running an experimental project. With the help of a vet, she attaches a small satellite tracker to the shells of a few adult turtles. Before each turtle goes back into the sea, Maya inserts a new battery into the tracker and activates it. Once the tracker is activated, it sends a signal every time the animal comes up to the surface to breathe. Since the project is experimental, nobody knows yet how long the trackers will last. Still, the information is crucial, because it shows where the turtles feed and which parts of the ocean are most dangerous for them.

Sometimes the volunteers find an animal that is sick or hurt. Last week they found a young turtle lying still on the beach. Its breathing was slow and weak. Maya drove it to the turtle hospital, where the vet examined it and made a quick diagnosis: the turtle had swallowed a piece of plastic. After a small operation, its breathing became normal again, and the vet said that the diagnosis had come just in time.

For Maya, though, the most important work is prevention. Saving one sick animal is wonderful, but prevention can save thousands. It means fewer plastic bags, fewer bright lights near the beach at night and slower boats along the coast. "Prevention is less exciting than a rescue," she says, "but it is crucial."

Questions:
What do the volunteers do every morning?
They patrol the beach and look for turtle tracks in the sand.
Why must the volunteers never interact with the animals?
When people try to interact with a wild animal, they usually do more harm than good.
What does Maya do before a turtle goes back into the sea?
She inserts a new battery into the tracker and activates it.
What was the diagnosis of the young turtle?
The diagnosis was that it had swallowed a piece of plastic.
Why does Maya think prevention is crucial?
She thinks it is crucial because saving one animal is wonderful, but prevention can save thousands.

lessons.title: The Sand Castle Contest
lessons.summary: Two cousins build an emperor on a throne of sand and win a friendly contest on the beach.
lessons.text:
Every August, the small town of Bayport, on the coast of Connecticut, holds a sand castle contest on its main beach. Anyone can take part, and the winners receive a silver trophy in the shape of a bucket. For the last three years, the Grant family has won the trophy. They have reigned over the contest for so long that people call them "the royal family of the beach."

This year two cousins, Ben and Olivia, decided that the reign of the Grant family had to end. The year before, they had finished second, only a few points behind. "This year we will have our revenge," said Ben, who was 14. Olivia laughed. "A friendly revenge," she said. "We just want to build something better."

For weeks they planned their design in secret. They drew it on paper in Olivia's kitchen and spoke about it only in whispers. Ben called it "our great conspiracy," and he enjoyed the conspiracy almost as much as the building itself. Their idea was bold: not a castle, but an emperor sitting on a huge throne, with the sea behind him.

On the day of the contest, 20 teams arrived at sunrise, and each team had four hours. Their strongest competitor, of course, was the Grant family, who began to build a tall castle with towers and bridges. Ben kept looking over at the competitor's castle until Olivia told him to stop. "Don't worry about the other teams," she said. "Worry about the emperor's nose."

The throne was the hardest part. They used wet sand and pressed it hard with their hands, so that the throne would not fall. Then Olivia shaped the emperor's face, with a long beard and a serious expression, and Ben added a crown made of shells. Children who walked past stopped to stare. One little boy pointed at the emperor's beard and said that the emperor looked like his grandfather. Everyone found this hilarious, and the cousins laughed so hard that they had to sit down. Even the boy's grandfather thought it was hilarious.

At the end of the day, the judges announced three nominations for the main prize: the Grant castle, a sea monster built by two grandmothers, and the emperor on his throne. The cousins were happy just to receive a nomination. Then the head judge said that the trophy went to the emperor.

The Grants were the first to shake their hands. "Our reign is over," said Mr. Grant with a smile. "Enjoy yours."

Questions:
Who had won the trophy for the last three years?
The Grant family had won it.
Why did Ben talk about revenge?
He talked about revenge because the year before, he and Olivia had finished second.
What did Ben call the secret plan?
He called it "our great conspiracy."
What did the cousins build?
They built an emperor sitting on a huge throne, with the sea behind him.
Who was their strongest competitor?
Their strongest competitor was the Grant family.
What did people find hilarious?
They found it hilarious when a little boy said that the emperor looked like his grandfather.

lessons.title: Caught by the Rising Sea
lessons.summary: A hiker on the coast of Maine is trapped by the rising water and is rescued by a Coast Guard helicopter.
lessons.text:
On a bright Saturday in September, Sam Turner went on a hike along the coast of Maine. He had planned the hike for weeks. The path followed the tops of the cliffs for 12 miles, with wide views over the Gulf of Maine, the great body of water that lies between Massachusetts and Canada. Sam packed water, a warm jacket and a box of cold pasta, which was his favorite lunch on a long hike.

Around noon he reached a small beach at the bottom of the cliffs. The sea had pulled back a long way, and wide flat rocks lay open to the sky. Sam climbed down to eat his pasta by the water. It was so quiet and beautiful that he forgot about the time. He walked farther and farther along the rocks, looking at shells and little pools of water.

When he finally looked back, his heart jumped. The sea was no longer in retreat. It had turned, and it was coming back fast. The water had already covered the rocks between him and the path, so he could not retreat the way he had come. The cliffs behind him were too steep to climb.

For a moment Sam felt pure terror. The wind began to whip the water into white waves, and cold drops whipped across his face. He forced himself to breathe slowly and think. He had once read that in an emergency, the worst thing you can do is let terror make your decisions. He climbed onto the highest rock he could find and took out his phone. To his great relief, it had a signal, and he called for help.

About 40 minutes later, he heard a loud noise above the wind. A red and white Coast Guard helicopter appeared over the cliffs. The helicopter stayed in the air above him, and a rescue worker came down on a cable. She fixed a strong belt around Sam, and together they were lifted up into the helicopter. Below them, the waves were already breaking over the rock where he had been standing.

At the hospital, a doctor checked Sam and said that he was cold but healthy. "It is a miracle that your phone worked down there," she said. Sam agreed that it felt like a miracle. He also knew that he had made a simple mistake. Now, before every hike, he checks when the sea will come in. He still takes cold pasta for lunch, but he eats it on the path, high above the water.

Questions:
Where did Sam go on his hike?
He went on a hike along the cliffs on the coast of Maine, with views over the Gulf of Maine.
What did Sam take for lunch?
He took a box of cold pasta.
Why could Sam not retreat the way he had come?
He could not retreat because the water had already covered the rocks between him and the path.
What did Sam do instead of letting terror decide for him?
He climbed onto the highest rock and called for help with his phone.
How was Sam rescued?
A Coast Guard helicopter came, and a rescue worker lifted him up on a cable.
What does Sam do now before every hike?
He checks when the sea will come in.

lessons.title: Whales off the Oregon Coast
lessons.summary: A woman takes her teenage nephew whale watching in the Pacific Northwest, and he draws the whale they see.
lessons.text:
Last spring I took my sister's son, Leo, on a whale-watching trip off the coast of Oregon. Leo is 15. He spends most of his free time drawing characters from anime, the cartoons from Japan that he loves, and he rarely looks up from his drawings. I hoped that a day at sea would show him something as exciting as anime.

We stayed in Depoe Bay, a small town in the Pacific Northwest. Early in the morning we took a taxi to the port, because our hotel was too far away to walk. "If you are lucky," the driver said, "you will see a whale breach. That means it jumps almost completely out of the water."

The boat was small. As soon as we left the shore, my phone lost its reception. Leo complained for a minute that he had no reception either. Then he put his phone in his pocket and watched the sea.

Our guide, a young scientist named Kim, explained that thousands of gray whales pass along this coast every spring on their long journey north. "Their journey is a remarkable phenomenon," she said. "They travel more than 10,000 miles every year." She also told us about the killer whales of the Northwest, which eat mainly salmon. Many rivers in the region have dams, and the dams make it hard for salmon to swim up the rivers to lay their eggs. Fewer salmon means less food for the whales. "Some dams have been removed," Kim said, "and the salmon are slowly coming back."

Then, about a mile from the shore, a gray whale rose out of the water right in front of us. Its huge body stood almost straight up in the air for a second, and then it fell back with a crash that threw water over the boat. It was stunning. Nobody on the boat said a word. A minute later the whale breached again, and everyone cheered.

Kim took photos of its tail. Each whale has its own marks, she explained, and scientists keep a catalog of them, so that they can recognize the same animal year after year. She checked the catalog on her phone and smiled. This whale was already in the catalog. It had been seen near Depoe Bay for eight years.

That evening Leo drew the whale in the anime style he loves, with huge shining eyes. The drawing was stunning, too, and it now hangs on my wall.

Questions:
What does Leo spend most of his free time doing?
He spends it drawing characters from anime.
What phenomenon did Kim describe?
She described the long journey of the gray whales, which is a remarkable phenomenon.
How did they get to the port?
They took a taxi, because the hotel was too far away to walk.
What does it mean when a whale breaches?
It means that the whale jumps almost completely out of the water.
Why do dams cause problems for the killer whales of the Northwest?
The dams make it hard for salmon to swim up the rivers, and fewer salmon means less food for the whales.
Why do scientists keep a catalog of the whales?
They keep a catalog so that they can recognize the same animal year after year.

lessons.title: A Visit to the Harbor Museum
lessons.summary: A short guide to a small museum that tells the history of a New England fishing town.
lessons.text:
If you visit Marbury, a small fishing town on the coast of Massachusetts, do not miss the Harbor Museum. It stands in an old brick building by the water and tells the story of the town, from its first wooden houses to the modern fishing boats of today. Here are some of the highlights.

The visit begins with a long timeline painted on the wall of the first room. The timeline starts in 1640, when the first families settled here, and it ends with a photo of the harbor taken last year. As you follow the timeline from left to right, you can see how a few small houses grew into a busy port.

In the second room you will find the workshop of a cooper. A cooper is a person who makes barrels, and 150 years ago coopers were among the most important workers in town. Fish was packed in salt and stored in barrels, so every boat needed dozens of them. On Saturdays a volunteer shows how a cooper bent the wood and held it together with metal rings.

The next room explains the ice harvest. Before electric refrigerators, people cut ice from frozen lakes in winter and stored it in buildings with thick walls. The winter harvest of ice allowed the boats to keep fish fresh for many days at sea. Old photos show men and horses harvesting ice on a lake near the town.

Another of the highlights is a model of a sailing ship with thin sheets of copper on its bottom. Small sea creatures used to eat holes in wooden ships, and the copper protected the wood. The copper also made the ships faster, because less sea life could grow on them.

The last room shows how the town's money was made. Some merchants became very wealthy, and their large houses, built with the earnings from fish and trade, still stand on Main Street. Ordinary fishermen, however, were far from wealthy. Their earnings depended on the catch: after each trip, the money was divided among the crew, so a bad trip meant small earnings for everyone.

Finally, do not miss the glass case of old newspapers. My favorite part is the classified section. One classified advertisement from 1885 offers work on a fishing boat for "strong young men who are not afraid of the cold." As you read the classified ads, you can almost hear the old town.

Questions:
What is painted on the wall of the first room?
A long timeline of the town, from 1640 to last year, is painted there.
What did a cooper do?
A cooper made barrels, which were needed to store fish packed in salt.
Why was the winter harvest of ice important?
It allowed the boats to keep fish fresh for many days at sea.
Why did ships have copper on their bottoms?
The copper protected the wood from small sea creatures and made the ships faster.
Why were the earnings of ordinary fishermen often small?
Their earnings depended on the catch, so a bad trip meant small earnings for everyone.
What can you find in the classified section of the old newspapers?
You can find old advertisements, such as an offer of work on a fishing boat from 1885.

lessons.title: Who Is the Harbor For?
lessons.summary: A local columnist writes calmly about a plan for a new marina and what the town should do next.
lessons.text:
Who Is the Harbor For?
By Daniel Reyes

Anyone who has walked along our harbor early in the morning knows the scene: fishing boats coming home, men and women carrying their catch to the trucks, the smell of salt and wet rope. This is the heart of Westbrook. That is why so many people were worried when a company from New York came to the town council last spring to propose a new marina.

The company proposes to build 200 places for private boats along the east side of the harbor, where many fishing boats now stay. It also proposes a hotel and several restaurants. Supporters say the marina would bring visitors and money. Others fear that the fishing boats would slowly be pushed out.

The council hired a consultant to study the plan. The consultant's report, published last month, is careful and fair. It says the marina could create 80 jobs, but it also says that the fishing boats would lose about a third of their space. The report adds that the Army Corps of Engineers would have to approve any digging in the harbor, and the Corps usually needs at least two years to decide.

The Westbrook Fishermen's Federation, which represents about 60 local boats, has asked the council for a suspension of the plan. In a letter, the federation said that a suspension of one year would give everyone time to think. Last week the council agreed, and the suspension begins in January.

I welcome this decision. It is my firm conviction that our harbor can serve a dual purpose: it can welcome visitors and still be a place where people work. Other towns on this coast have done both. A harbor with a dual purpose is not a dream; it is possible, provided that we plan it well.

There is also a psychological side to this question, which the consultant does not mention. When we look at the harbor and see working boats, we feel connected to the generations who built this town. That psychological connection is hard to measure, but it is real, and it is worth protecting.

So I would like to propose something myself. During the suspension, the council should initiate a series of public meetings, where fishermen, business owners and other residents can talk to each other directly. If the council does not initiate these meetings, the federation should. Our harbor belongs to all of us, and we should decide its future together, with patience and conviction.

Questions:
What did the company from New York propose?
It proposed a new marina with 200 places for private boats, a hotel and several restaurants.
What did the consultant's report say?
It said the marina could create 80 jobs, but the fishing boats would lose about a third of their space.
Why did the federation ask for a suspension of the plan?
It asked for a suspension because one year would give everyone time to think.
What is Daniel's firm conviction?
He believes that the harbor can serve a dual purpose, for visitors and for people who work.
What psychological side does Daniel describe?
He says that seeing working boats makes people feel connected to the generations who built the town.
What should the council initiate during the suspension?
It should initiate a series of public meetings.
